tone_statements.quote: The kasɩm has a three-tone system: low tone, mid tone, high tone. These tones can succeed each other and give rise to different combinations. Normally it does not mark the tones in spelling kasɩm (see 'Guide to spelling kasɩm') with the exception of a few grammatical words that carry a high tone (see comment in this web Site under «Entries»). [...] In the document ‘The kasɩm grammar élémentaire’, in part 5 (the verb, pages 71 ff.), we have indicated the grammatical tonal changes of the verbs in brackets (e.g. [bà] low tone, [bā] mid tone, [bá] high tone, [bǎ] rising tone).
tone_statements.summary: 3 level tones L/M/H (plus rising contour on verbs), lexical and grammatical function (verb aspect/polarity by tone); tone unmarked in orthography except a few H-toned grammatical words; no statement on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Awedoba, A. K. 1990. Kasem tones and orthography. Journal of West African Languages 20(2): 31-46.
tone_statements.quote: Four basic tones have been identified (Callow 1965) and include three level tones: low [*], mid [-] and high [*]. The fourth tone is designated ‘rising’ tone [4]. Other contour tonal realisations occur as a result of the loss of tone bearing segmental units and the subsequent attachment of the following unit’s tone to a contiguous unit. … I agree with him that the domain of tone is a unit higher than the syllable which may comprise between one and four, … possibly five, syllables; but the unit may also be a full word or part of a word.

sources.citation: Pike, Kenneth L. 1966. Tagmemic and matrix linguistics applied to selected African languages. Final report. (ERIC ED010547; Kasem appendices by John & Kathleen Callow).
sources.note: Kasem material is clause/serial-construction and nominal/verbal matrices only; the volume's only word-stress rule (stress on highest-toned syllable) is in the Agbo (Legbo) appendix, not Kasem. Cites Callow 1965 'Collected field reports on the phonology of Kasem' as the Kasem phonology source.

sources.note: scanned. Treats the grammatical word as a phonological unit defined by vowel harmony and the distribution of tone and nasality (fn. 12: 'vowel harmony, nasalisation, and pitch'); stress is never mentioned.

sources.citation: Awedoba, A. K. 1990. Kasem tones and orthography. Journal of West African Languages 20(2): 31-46.
sources.note: Scanned; scanned with tesseract. Describes the tone system (levels, grammatical tone, no downdrift), segment inventory (19 C, 10 V), CV syllable preference, short words; 'accent' only in the sense of French orthographic diacritics. No statement about stress.

tone.quote: Four basic tones have been identified (Callow 1965) and include three level tones: low [*], mid [-] and high [*]. The fourth tone is designated ‘rising’ tone [4]. Other contour tonal realisations occur as a result of the loss of tone bearing segmental units and the subsequent attachment of the following unit’s tone to a contiguous unit. … I agree with him that the domain of tone is a unit higher than the syllable which may comprise between one and four, … possibly five, syllables; but the unit may also be a full word or part of a word.
tone.says: Four tones: low, mid, high and rising, each carried by a 'bar' (1-5 syllables, a word or part of one) and spread over its syllables; no downdrift or downstep seen; Burkina accounts count 3 levels.
